edges.effect_quant: The best cohort evidence suggests prostate-selective alpha antagonists modestly but meaningfully increase falls in older men, likely via first-dose or early-treatment hypotension. In a nationwide Korean cohort, subtype-specific alpha antagonists were associated with an OR of 1.80 for falls versus matched nonusers, and in a large Ontario study of men aged 66 and older starting prostate-selective alpha antagonists, the 90-day odds ratio for falls was 1.14 and for hypotension was 1.80. Because most exposed men in that cohort received tamsulosin, the signal is highly relevant to real-world tamsulosin prescribing.
edges.population: older men treated with tamsulosin or similar prostate-selective alpha antagonists for lower urinary tract symptoms or benign prostatic hyperplasia
edges.mechanism: Tamsulosin can reduce vascular tone enough to provoke orthostatic symptoms, especially soon after initiation, dose changes, dehydration, or concurrent antihypertensive use. Even though it is relatively prostate-selective, the remaining alpha-1 blockade can still translate into dizziness, head trauma, and falls in vulnerable older men.
edges.summary: This is a credible harmful edge, though the absolute excess risk is not enormous. Large observational studies consistently show a higher short-term risk of falls, fractures, or hypotension-related injury after starting prostate-selective alpha antagonists, and tamsulosin dominates prescribing in those real-world datasets.
edges.caveats: Most of the strongest evidence is for the alpha-antagonist class or cohorts in which tamsulosin is the predominant agent rather than an isolated tamsulosin-only randomized comparison. The signal also seems front-loaded around treatment initiation, so it should be interpreted more as an early orthostatic hazard than as a constant large risk over years of stable use.
